record.name: Aleksandar Paunović
record.title: Professor Emeritus
record.bio: Aleksandar Paunović received his undergraduate and master's degrees in information systems from the Faculty of Economics in Subotica, University of Novi Sad, in 1982 and 1986 respectively, and completed his doctorate at the same institution in 1993 with a dissertation on internal control systems in Yugoslav banking. He joined the faculty as an assistant professor in 1994 and was promoted to full professor in 2004, retiring to emeritus status in 2019. His research concentrated on audit trail design, tamper-evident log architectures, and append-only data structures for compliance monitoring in banking, insurance, and healthcare. He taught courses on database systems, business informatics, and internal audit technology for over two decades, supervising more than thirty master's theses. He conducted applied work using IBM mainframe audit facilities, early relational database log mechanisms, and later column-store systems available at the faculty computing laboratory.
record.industry_experience: Between 1999 and 2005, Paunović served as an external technical advisor to the IT audit function of a mid-sized Serbian commercial bank during its preparation for National Bank of Serbia supervisory examinations, advising on log retention infrastructure and audit trail documentation. He has also provided expert witness testimony in two civil proceedings involving disputed electronic audit records.
record.notes: Professor Paunović is retired and explicitly limits his external engagement to consulting; he will not join grant project teams or take on student supervision. His most current technical knowledge covers architectures up to approximately 2016; the 2021 and 2024 papers were co-authored at the invitation of former students and should not be taken as evidence of active ongoing research. He is most useful as a domain expert on regulatory history, audit log design principles, and compliance frameworks for Serbian and regional financial institutions. Engagements should be time-limited and do not require laboratory access.
